title: Standing for Delivery: a Dominant Copper Position, and $150 Million Neither Admitted Nor Denied

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The motive the order records is loss, not greed: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper." The manipulation began as a way of not realising what had already been lost.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was physical control of a market through its delivery mechanism. During 1995 and 1996 Sumitomo "established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME", and "In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was the price itself. A dominant holder standing for delivery produces a quoted price that looks like scarcity, and the order finds the effect "directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels" — prices paid by everyone who used copper, none of whom could see the position producing them.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is stated as the object of the exercise: the actions were taken "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The settlement is the containment and its shape is worth reading closely. $150 million in total, of which $125 million was an immediate civil penalty and $25 million was escrowed for up to four years for restitution to injured persons — reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. The findings were "neither admitted nor denied". And the chairperson's statement credits the company for "constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", which is a regulator explaining why the number is what it is.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A metals exchange whose price is set by physical delivery against warrants, and a cross-border market in which the dominant position sat on one exchange while the affected prices were in several jurisdictions.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The cooperation precedent the Commission emphasises — "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government" — and the assertion of US jurisdiction over manipulation conducted on a London exchange.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Speculative losses created the need to support the price; supporting the price required a larger position; the larger position made the price more artificial and the eventual unwind more damaging, which is the position the trader was trying not to have.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That one rogue trader secretly cornered the world copper market for a decade while his employer knew nothing, and that regulators never got to the bottom of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission’s order is against the corporation, not an individual: it found "that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", acting "through its agent or agents". That is a finding of corporate liability, which is the opposite of the lone-rogue framing. It is also narrower in time than the legend — 1995 and 1996, not a decade. But the dossier must not overstate it in the other direction either: the order settled the matter by consent and "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings", so this is a settled regulatory finding rather than an adjudicated verdict, and no individual is found liable in it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC order of 11 May 1998, settled by consent, finding that Sumitomo manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996 in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Large and dominant LME futures positions; standing for delivery on a significant percentage of maturing contracts in autumn 1995; a resulting dominant and controlling cash and futures position that directly and predictably drove US cash and futures prices to artificially high levels; and the express purpose of creating an artificially high price and nearby premium to profit on liquidating the futures portfolio and LME warrants. $150 million total: $125 million immediate civil penalty, $25 million escrowed up to four years for restitution. Findings neither admitted nor denied.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "CFTC Files and Settles Action Against Sumitomo Corporation for Manipulating the Copper Market in 1995-96", Release 4144-98, 11 May 1998
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The Commission issued an order "in connection with settling the matter by consent, finding that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", in which "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings". THE MECHANISM AS THE ORDER DESCRIBES IT: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper. In particular, during 1995 and 1996, Sumitomo, acting through its agent or agents, established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME. In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position, which directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels." The purpose is stated: "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants", in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. THE PENALTY: "a total of $150 million", of which "$125 million will be paid as a civil monetary penalty immediately" and "The remaining $25 million will be placed into escrow for a period of up to four years" available "to provide restitution to persons injured by Sumitomo's unlawful conduct", reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. CFTC Chairperson Brooksley Born called it "an historic moment in the Commission's work to protect the people of the United States, the United States cash and futures markets and their participants against market manipulation", noting also "the credit Sumitomo deserves for constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", and describing "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government". A settled consent order whose findings were neither admitted nor denied.
